---
title: "mv_ask(): from a sentence to a tested R script"
description: >
  How mv_ask() turns a plain-language request into a complete IRT analysis
  script, with worked examples and benchmark results for Claude, GPT and
  local Ollama models.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

Many people who need an IRT analysis know what they want to find out but not
which functions, arguments and checks get them there. `mv_ask()` closes that
gap. You describe the analysis in a sentence, and mirtverse writes the full,
commented R script: reading the data, recoding missing values, fitting and
checking the model, testing for DIF, scoring, plotting and reporting. You read
the script, change it if you like, and then run or save it.

This article explains how `mv_ask()` works, walks through examples, and reports
how accurately it understands requests with each of the supported language
models.

```{r setup}
library(mirtverse)
```

## How it works

```{r, echo = FALSE}
# Embedded as a data URI so the figure travels with the page
htmltools::img(
  src = knitr::image_uri("figures/mv-ask-workflow.svg"), width = "100%",
  alt = paste("Workflow of mv_ask(): your request and a summary of your data are",
              "turned into an analysis plan by the keyword parser or an optional AI",
              "model; the plan is checked against the data and tested templates",
              "write the R script, which you run or save."))
```

`mv_ask()` follows a **hybrid design**: a language model (or a built-in
keyword parser) decides *what* to do, and mirtverse decides *how* to do it.

1. **Summarise the data.** `profile_data()` describes each column: its type,
   number of distinct values, range, share missing and likely role (item,
   grouping variable, ID or response time). Individual responses are never
   part of this summary.
2. **Understand the request.** The request and the summary go to the
   understanding step. By default this is a keyword parser that runs offline
   and needs no setup. If you connect a model with `mv_ask_setup()`, Claude,
   GPT or a local Ollama model does this step instead. The model never writes
   code. It fills in a structured form with a fixed set of choices: which
   columns are items, which model, how many dimensions, which grouping
   variable, which missing-value codes and which outputs.
3. **Check the plan.** The filled-in form becomes an `mv_plan()` object, which
   is checked against your data before any code is written. Do the columns
   exist? Does the grouping variable have at least two groups? Is a 2PL being
   asked of items with more than two categories? Problems are reported in
   plain language, and anything mirtverse assumed is listed.
4. **Write the script.** Tested templates turn the plan into R code that uses
   only mirt and mirtverse functions with checked arguments. The same
   templates power the code export in the [workbench](workbench.html).
5. **Run or save.** Nothing runs until you ask. `run_script(scr, check = TRUE)`
   first runs the whole script on simulated data shaped like yours, so any
   error shows up before your real data are touched.

Because the language model only chooses among options that mirtverse already
knows how to code, a model cannot invent a function or an argument that does
not exist. The worst a misunderstanding can do is produce a valid script for a
different analysis than the one you meant, and the printed plan makes that
easy to spot.

## Examples

The examples use a small simulated data set: 800 students, twelve 0/1 items
(`Q1` to `Q12`), a gender column and a student ID. They use the built-in
keyword parser (`provider = "none"`) so that this page builds without an API
key. With an AI model connected, the same requests work, and so does much
freer wording.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
a <- matrix(rlnorm(12, 0.2, 0.25))
d <- matrix(rnorm(12))
mydata <- data.frame(student_id = 1:800, simdata(a, d, 800, itemtype = "2PL"),
                     gender = rep(c("F", "M"), 400))
names(mydata)[2:13] <- paste0("Q", 1:12)
```

### A complete analysis in one sentence

```{r}
scr <- mv_ask("Fit a 2PL, check DIF by gender and make a report",
              data = mydata, provider = "none")
scr
```

The printout has three parts: the plan (what will be done), the assumptions
mirtverse made (here, that `Q1` to `Q12` are the items because they look like
item responses), and the script itself.

### Refining a script

Pass the script back with the change you want. The rest of the plan is kept.

```{r}
scr <- mv_ask(scr, "use a 3PL instead and save EAP scores to scores.csv")
scr$plan
```

### Letting mirtverse choose the model

When you don't name a model, mirtverse compares the candidates with
`select_model()` and keeps the best one.

```{r}
mv_ask("Which IRT model fits my data best? Explain the results in plain language.",
       data = mydata, provider = "none")
```

### Missing-value codes and a subset of items

```{r}
coded <- mydata
coded$Q3[c(5, 17, 40)] <- 9
mv_ask("Rasch model for Q1 to Q10 only; 9 means missing. Give me person scores.",
       data = coded, provider = "none")$plan
```

### Using an AI model

Connect a model once. The key is asked for in a masked prompt and stored in
your `.Renviron` file or the system keychain, never in scripts or reports.

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mv_ask_setup("claude")                         # Anthropic Claude, your own key
mv_ask_setup("openai")                         # OpenAI GPT, your own key
mv_ask_setup("ollama", model = "qwen3.8:27b")  # free, runs on your computer
```

After that, `mv_ask()` uses the model automatically, and requests can be as
loose as you would write them to a colleague:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mv_ask("I want to know whether boys and girls with the same ability answer
        the items differently, and I need a report for my committee",
       data = mydata)
```

### Seeing exactly what is sent

`dry_run = TRUE` prints what would be sent to the model without sending it.
With `anonymize = TRUE`, column names are replaced by `V1`, `V2`, ... (also
inside your request) and category labels are dropped. mirtverse maps the names
back on your computer.

```{r}
mv_ask("check DIF by gender", data = mydata, anonymize = TRUE, dry_run = TRUE)
```

### Writing a plan by hand

The plan is an ordinary R object, so you can skip the request entirely:

```{r}
pl <- mv_plan(items = "Q1:Q10", model = "Rasch",
              steps = c("describe", "fitcheck", "scores", "report"))
mv_ask(data = mydata, plan = pl)
```

## How accurate is it?

We wrote 100 requests of the kind users actually type, from "1PL please" to
"Fit a 2PL to my data, check DIF by gender, and make a report", each with the
plan a careful analyst would choose. A few are deliberately vague (such as
"check DIF" when the data have several possible grouping columns), and the
right response to these is to ask a question rather than guess. The requests
and expected plans are in
[`inst/benchmark/ask-requests.csv`](https://github.com/okanbulut/mirtverse/blob/main/inst/benchmark/ask-requests.csv).

A plan counts as **fully correct** only if every field matches: whether a
question was needed, the model, the number of dimensions, the grouping
variable, the missing-value codes, the items and the analysis steps.

```{r, echo = FALSE}
bench <- data.frame(
  Parser = c("Claude (claude-opus-5-5)", "OpenAI GPT (gpt-5.6-terra)",
             "Ollama: Qwen 3 8B",
             "Built-in keyword parser*"),
  `Fully correct` = c(95, 90, 35, 98),
  Question = c(96, 98, 83, 100),
  Model = c(99, 97, 91, 100),
  Dimensions = c(100, 100, 100, 100),
  Group = c(99, 99, 99, 100),
  Missing = c(100, 100, 100, 100),
  Items = c(100, 100, 100, 100),
  Steps = c(98, 94, 46, 98),
  check.names = FALSE)
knitr::kable(bench, align = "lrrrrrrrr",
             caption = "Percentage of the 100 benchmark requests understood correctly.")
```

\* The keyword parser's patterns were tuned on these same 100 requests, so its
score is an upper bound. On new wording it will do worse, which is where the
AI models earn their place.

What the results show:

* **Claude** understood 95 of 100 requests completely, and no field fell
  below 96%. Its misses were mostly about whether to ask a clarifying question
  and which outputs to include.
* **GPT** reached 90%. Its weakest field was the analysis steps (94%): it
  added or left out outputs, such as a report or plots, more often than
  Claude.
* **Local models (Ollama)** keep everything on your computer and cost
  nothing per request, but small models struggle. Qwen 3 8B got the model,
  items, group and missing codes right almost always, yet chose the right
  set of analysis steps only 46% of the time, so only 35% of its plans were
  fully correct. Always read the printed plan before running a script
  written with a small local model.
* **Every field except steps and questions is at least 97% for all parsers.**
  Choosing the model, the items, the group and the missing codes is easy.
  The harder part is reading how much the user wants done.

To run the benchmark yourself, for example to try another Ollama model:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
mirtverse:::ask_benchmark("claude")
mirtverse:::ask_benchmark("openai")
mirtverse:::ask_benchmark("ollama", model = "qwen3:8b")
```

Each run sends the 100 requests with the column summary of a simulated data
set. With Claude or GPT this costs roughly one or two US dollars. A local
model costs nothing but takes longer: from about ten minutes to an hour,
depending on the model and your computer.

## Privacy in brief

* Individual responses are never sent. The model sees your request and the
  column summary from `profile_data()`.
* `anonymize = TRUE` hides column names and category labels.
* `dry_run = TRUE` shows exactly what would be sent.
* With Ollama, nothing leaves your computer at all.
* Without any setup, the keyword parser runs fully offline.
